claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a reported hierarchical heterostructure with multilevel chemical fluctuations.
A physics-informed ML framework using simulation-derived mesoscale descriptors and microstructural imaging data will accurately predict Young’s modulus for hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
The proposed framework will accurately predict yield strength for hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
The proposed framework will accurately predict fracture toughness for hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
The model will use descriptors extracted from mesoscale phase-field simulations and experimental microstructural imaging.
Phase-boundary distributions, defect densities, and chemical-fluctuation metrics capture the hierarchical heterostructure’s effects on local stress fields.
Constraining ML with physical, simulation-derived, and imaging-derived descriptors reduces the model’s search space.
The descriptor constraints improve mapping between local microstructural features and macroscopic mechanical response.
The descriptor-constrained framework lowers computational demand relative to conventional first-principles, CALPHAD, and standalone ML approaches.
The framework will reduce prediction error by approximately 15–30% relative to conventional first-principles/CALPHAD and standalone ML models.
The framework will reduce simulation time by a factor of 2–10.
Explicit first-principles evaluation of alloy fracture or yield strength is generally beyond available DFT implementations.
First-principles simulations remain challenging for disordered multi-principal-element alloys.
Conventional ML models require extensive high-fidelity data.
Conventional approaches have limited accuracy for fracture toughness.
The method may become unreliable if processing or testing substantially alters the hierarchical heterostructure.
The method may become unreliable at extreme temperatures or strain rates if the selected descriptors fail to represent emergent microstructural features.
The exact accuracy and efficiency gains are uncertain until the framework is validated across more samples and testing conditions.
